drills.trains: The long-then-short cadence, and the habit of judging instead of describing in the short slot.
drills.do: Write 20 paragraph-pairs. Each pair is one sentence of 25-35 words carrying an action, then one sentence of 3-6 words. The short sentence may only judge, negate, question, or name a cost. It may not describe anything.
drills.test: Delete the short sentence. The paragraph should lose meaning, not information. If it loses information, you wrote description.

drills.trains: Handling unfamiliar terms without slowing down. His single most-grown habit: up 5x since 2014.
drills.do: Take 25 technical or foreign terms from your own world. Write one sentence each, glossing the term with a 1-6 word noun phrase inside paired commas. Never 'which means'. Never parentheses.
drills.test: Delete every gloss. All 25 sentences must still parse and still be grammatical.

drills.trains: Grounding an abstraction in something physically present, then closing in four words.
drills.do: Write 15 micro-scenes. In each, someone explains an abstract idea, then points at or picks up something already in the scene, then delivers a verdict of four words or fewer.
drills.test: Cover the abstract instruction. The pointing plus the verdict must still teach the idea on their own.

drills.trains: His biggest compressor: dramatise only where somebody changes.
drills.do: Take a 1,200-word scene of yours with full dialogue. Any exchange conveying logistics, agreement, or procedure becomes one sentence of reported speech. Only exchanges where a character changes their mind keep quotation marks.
drills.test: Under 700 words, no plot information lost, and every remaining quoted line contains a decision or an emotion.

drills.trains: Untagged dialogue volleys. Trust in the reader.
drills.do: Write a two-character argument of 20 turns. Only 'said' is allowed, at most 5 times. Zero adverbs. At most 3 physical beats, each carrying information no line of dialogue does.
drills.test: Give it to someone else. They must always know who is speaking.

drills.trains: Quantification as intensity. Adjectives are for objects; numbers are for feelings.
drills.do: Take 30 sentences of yours containing very, extremely, incredibly, huge, enormous, countless, endless. Replace every intensifier with a specific number, distance, duration, or count.
drills.test: Read both aloud. If the numbered version feels flatter, your number was too round. Pick an odd one: 41 headlines, 2,500 miles, 48 minutes.

drills.trains: Subject-first, verb-early, right-branching syntax. He cut front-loaded participles 25%.
drills.do: Write 500 words in which no sentence delays its grammatical subject past word six, and no fronted subordinate clause runs longer than six words.
drills.test: Mark every subject and count. Zero violations allowed.

drills.trains: Placing the surprise in terminal position, where he always puts it.
drills.do: Take 20 of your sentences where the key information sits mid-sentence. Rewrite each so the key word is the last word or inside the last three. You may not add words.
drills.test: Cover everything except the final three words of each. A reader should still guess what the sentence was about.

drills.trains: Withholding as a source of authority. This is where 'profound' actually comes from.
drills.do: Write 12 passages of 60-100 words. Each raises a question the reader wants answered, then declines it by a different mechanism: tautological dismissal, deferral to later, outsourcing to another source, naming competing versions without picking, asserting further reasons exist, declaring it unfathomable.
drills.test: Each refusal must make you sound like you know more, never less. If any reads as evasion, the surrounding prose lacked hard specifics.

drills.trains: The status transaction that makes a high idea feel reachable.
drills.do: List 12 abstract claims from your work. For each write one self-contained 40-70 word analogy from a domain humbler than the subject: kitchen, tamed animals, small children, weather, machines you have physically operated. End it and never return.
drills.test: No analogy mentioned twice. No vehicle from aviation, physics, war, neuroscience, or software. If you extended one past two sentences, you failed.

drills.trains: Awe without adjectives. He writes overwhelm as a cessation of motion.
drills.do: Write 10 moments of overwhelming significance. Banned: radiant, resplendent, magnificent, glorious, divine, awe-inspiring, breathtaking, ethereal, luminous. Each moment is built from a stopping of motion or sound, plus one specific material detail, plus one number.
drills.test: Read them cold. If any could be swapped into another of the ten without loss, the material detail was not specific enough.

drills.trains: Understatement at the peak. The clock re-anchors the reader exactly where the prose could inflate.
drills.do: Write 250 words on the most intense experience you have had. The final sentence must be a clock time, a date, or a measurement, and nothing else. Delete any sentence that summarises what it meant.
drills.test: Remove the final sentence: it should feel like it is still inflating. Restore it: it should stop dead.

drills.trains: Replacing emotional adjectives with self-measurement. His strongest anti-indulgence device.
drills.do: Describe a day of hard effort in 400 words. Banned: exhausting, gruelling, intense, overwhelming, painful, unbearable, incredible, amazing. Rate yourself out of ten on at least two axes, then argue with your own rating in one sentence.
drills.test: A reader can state your score on each axis and one reason you distrust it. If they can only report a feeling, you failed.

drills.trains: Disarming disbelief without arguing. The refusal to persuade is what buys credibility.
drills.do: Write 300 words on your least believable true experience. Four parts: plain narration with no persuasion; the three most likely rational explanations in your own voice; one piece of factual, non-boastful credential evidence; a close that explicitly does not ask to be believed.
drills.test: Give it to a skeptic. They must not raise an objection you did not already state.

drills.trains: Removing accusation from instruction. The most transferable single rule in the corpus.
drills.do: Take a draft. Rewrite every sentence naming a problem into 'we'. Rewrite every sentence giving an instruction into 'you'. Mark the one crossover point. Rewrite every ranked list into third person.
drills.test: One crossover. Zero instructions in 'we'. Zero diagnoses in 'you'. Zero ranked items in 'you'.

drills.trains: Authority without arrogance. The number is the credential.
drills.do: Before any claim strong enough to sound like a lecture, write one sentence of cost containing a number and zero adjectives. Then the claim. Then one scope-limit sentence starting 'I am not saying'. Order is fixed. Do ten.
drills.test: 'I lost ₹3.4 lakh' passes. 'I suffered a devastating loss' fails. Check every one.

drills.trains: The story-to-point transition, done his way.
drills.do: Collect ten small real stories: overheard remarks, client emails, something your brother said. End each on a line of speech. Then open the next paragraph by repeating that line verbatim, a colon, then the principle in twelve words or fewer.
drills.test: The repeated line is verbatim, and everything after the colon is 12 words or fewer.

drills.trains: The ending, which is where most writers fail.
drills.do: Take one finished piece. Write five different closes: title echoed as a question; two short imperatives; a conditional promise whose payoff is a state not a result; a definition landing of ten words or fewer; a reversal. Each 8-40 words, each sentence shorter than the last.
drills.test: None summarises the piece. None ends on a quotation. Pick one and delete the rest.

drills.trains: Question openings at the density of his short-form work.
drills.do: Open eight pieces with 3-4 questions, each strictly shorter than the last, questions 2 onward starting lowercase so the stack reads as one breath. Answer in the very next sentence. Keep two.
drills.test: Each question shorter than the last. Answer starts immediately. Every question is one the reader would already have asked.

drills.trains: Describing the overwhelming by inventory rather than adjective.
drills.do: Describe something beautiful in 200 words using a fixed directional scan, top-to-bottom or near-to-far, one component per clause, and only plain adjectives: small, full, fair, wide, bare, soft, dark. Include exactly one detail that contradicts what you expected, and say so.
drills.test: No word you would not also use to describe a chair. The contradicted expectation must be present - that line converts description into testimony.

drills.trains: Refusing the second high. Every peak is followed by something that costs you.
drills.do: Write five peaks of 150 words. After each, write a paragraph that admits a failure, reports a chore, names what the peak broke, or records a doubt. No peak may be followed by another peak or a summary of its meaning.
drills.test: With the follow-ups removed the peaks should read as boastful. With them restored, as reported.

drills.trains: Getting simpler as the stakes rise - the inversion almost nobody performs.
drills.do: Take your three most emotional passages and your most technical one. Compute mean sentence length and mean word length in characters for each.
drills.test: The emotional passages must score LOWER on both. Target peaks at 13-15 words per sentence and under 4.15 characters per word; exposition around 20. Rewrite until the numbers invert.

drills.trains: His simplicity engine: seven in ten words are one syllable, every book, for twelve years.
drills.do: On a finished draft: count monosyllables and push to 65% or more. Count sentences of 30+ words and push under 7%. Count commas per sentence and push under 1.1. Split anything with three or more commas.
drills.test: All three numbers met, measured in the Workbench, not estimated.

drills.trains: The connective repertoire, and killing silent drift.
drills.do: Take a 2,000-word draft. Tag every paragraph transition as one of: chronometric, return-to-scene, concessive, confession, restatement, anti-misreading, additive, resume, parallel-cut, amplifier. Enforce at least 40% chronometric, no other label over 20%, at least one of each.
drills.test: No paragraph begins with untagged drift. Every return from a digression carries an explicit re-entry marker or a timestamp.

drills.trains: The single highest-leverage deletion available. He cut 83% of his in a decade.
drills.do: Search every draft you have for a semicolon. Replace each with a full stop and repair the two halves so both stand alone. No exceptions.
drills.test: Zero semicolons. Then read aloud - the rhythm should feel faster even though you added no words.

drills.trains: The clearest single difference between his 2014 and 2024 books.
drills.do: Find the paragraph after a scene that explains what the scene meant. Keep its single best sentence. Move that sentence up inside the scene. Delete the rest of the paragraph.
drills.test: The scene must now carry the meaning on its own. If a reader misses the point, the sentence you kept was the wrong one - swap it, do not restore the paragraph.

drills.trains: Opening on a person, a fact, or a clock. Not one of his chapters opens on weather.
drills.do: Write 15 openings of two sentences each. Every one names a person, a hard fact, a date, or a clock time within the first six words, and contains a want or a refusal. Banned: weather, time of day as scenery, setting description, throat-clearing.
drills.test: Hand them to someone. They should know within six words who or what the piece is about.

drills.trains: His joke architecture, and the register control around it.
drills.do: Write ten jokes: exactly two speakers, 40-120 words, one line of setup narration, one or two exchanges, punchline spoken by the lower-status character, and the punchline is a literalism - someone takes a figure of speech at face value.
drills.test: The butt of every joke is the expert, the boss, or you. Never the reader. And if your subject is someone's body, money loss, or grief, you wrote zero jokes.

drills.trains: Deadpan timing as an arithmetic property.
drills.do: Write 20 three-sentence jokes where sentence lengths strictly descend, for example 7 words, then 3, then 4. Model: rhetorical question, flat two-word answer, short specifying tag.
drills.test: Count the words. Any sentence longer than the one before it fails. Remove the third sentence - the joke should get measurably worse.

drills.trains: Internalising his cadence without copying his words.
drills.do: Take a pattern of sentence lengths, for example 22-4-15-31-6-12-3. Write a paragraph of your own on any subject that matches it exactly, word for word in count. Do ten different patterns.
drills.test: Paste into the Workbench. The rhythm bars must match the target shape. This trains the ear that copywork trains, using your own sentences.

drills.trains: The third beat almost everyone skips, and the one that makes an image explain rather than illustrate.
drills.do: Take 15 abstract claims. For each write three sentences: the claim flat and under 15 words; a concrete physical image; then the claim again, restated using the image's own noun.
drills.test: Cover the first sentence. The third must still deliver the full claim on its own.

drills.trains: Specificity as evidence. He runs about 7 numerals per 1,000 words.
drills.do: Rewrite a 500-word passage to include: two clock times, one dimension in feet or inches, one price, three named objects (a specific plant, food, or brand), and two named people.
drills.test: A stranger could sketch the room and price the objects. Then delete every adjective - it should lose almost nothing.

drills.trains: Openings and closings as a matched system.
drills.do: Write eight openings and eight closings, unattached to anything. Openings: a person or hard fact in the first six words, containing a want or a refusal. Closings: one of exactly four types - open question, explicit handoff, second-person maxim, or a term earned as punchline.
drills.test: Shuffle all sixteen and hand them over. A reader must sort openings from closings with 100% accuracy.

drills.trains: His late-era rule: never interleave method with narrative.
drills.do: Take any piece of yours containing a numbered how-to. Pull every step out and put it at the end, or behind a link. Rewrite the narrative so it runs clean without them.
drills.test: The narrative must stand alone and still be worth reading. If it collapses, the prose was leaning on the list.

drills.trains: Handling disagreement without defending. He never wins an argument on the page.
drills.do: After your strongest claim, write the objection in the reader's voice, opened with 'You may ask' or 'I know some will say'. Then do not rebut it. Concede it and narrow your own claim instead. Do eight.
drills.test: Zero instances of 'but actually' or 'however this misses'. You narrowed your claim; you did not defend it.

drills.trains: Speed and reflex with the appositive gloss, until it stops being a decision.
drills.do: Fifty terms, fifty sentences, thirty minutes. Each term glossed inline with commas in 1-6 words. Do not stop to judge quality. Volume is the point.
drills.test: Fifty done inside the half hour. Then read them back and mark the ten that sound like teaching - those are the failures.
